Adsorbent / material: Biochars from rice straw, coconut husk, fish scale powder and spent tea leaves; pyrolysis at 200, 350, 450, 550 and 700 °C for 1 h
Experimental design / conditions: Comparative batch assay: 40 mL deionized water, 50 mg/L Dox, 1 g/L adsorbent, pH 7, 30 °C, 140 rpm, 4 h
Reported result: Rice-straw biochar prepared at 700 °C removed 97.29% Dox; rice-straw biochar prepared at 200 °C removed 58.51% under the comparative assay
Caveat / follow-up: Batch data at 50 mg/L initial Dox, not trace environmental concentrations. Keep comparison conditions attached.

Experimental design / conditions: Central composite design considered temperature 20–40 °C, time 15–300 min, pH 5–9, dose 0.5–10 g/L and Dox load 20–500 mg/L
Reported result: Predicted optimum: 30 °C, 165 min, pH 6.8, 6.6 g/L biochar and 408.3 mg/L Dox; predicted removal 100%, experimental response 99.92%
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 7, §3.4, Eq. (1), Table 3 and Fig. 4
Caveat / follow-up: High-concentration, high-dose batch condition; not proof of full-scale performance.

Experimental design / conditions: Kinetic method reports 250 mL reaction volume and 500 mg/L Dox load; sampled for 2 h. Kinetic dose is not clearly specified in that method paragraph
Reported result: Residual Dox declined sharply during the first 15 min and equilibrium was reported around 45 min; experimentally obtained q_e = 26.33 mg/g
Caveat / follow-up: Do not infer unspecified kinetic dose or pH. The concentration is far above trace environmental concentrations.

Experimental design / conditions: Same kinetic study; some operating conditions are not fully specified in the supplied main-text methods
Reported result: Pseudo-second-order fit: R² = 1 and model q_e = 26.45 mg/g, close to experimental q_e = 26.33 mg/g. Pseudo-first-order fit: R² = 0.9872, model q_e = 2.58 mg/g
Value / units: PSO q_e 26.45 mg/g; observed q_e 26.33 mg/g; PFO q_e 2.58 mg/g; R² values 1 and 0.9872
Caveat / follow-up: Model fit does not prove a unique adsorption mechanism. Keep calculated and observed q_e separate.

Experimental design / conditions: Initial Dox loads 500–2000 mg/L; 6 g/L biochar; pH 6.8; 30 °C; 120 rpm; 45 min
Reported result: Langmuir-fitted q_max reported as 200 mg/g. Freundlich fit reports K_f = 602.56 and n = 2.78; the paper reports R² = 0.991 for the Freundlich linear fit
Caveat / follow-up: Fitted q_max is not the same endpoint as observed q_e or percent removal. The isotherm uses high initial loads.

Experimental design / conditions: Authors report Dox initial load of 600 mg/L in distilled, tap, river, pond and seawater matrices
Reported result: Removal reported as: distilled 99.74%; tap 99.13%; river 98.11%; pond 97.13%; seawater 96.84%
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 10, §3.8; Fig. S3/Table S1 are referenced but not included in the uploaded file
Caveat / follow-up: These are water-matrix tests at high Dox load, not validation in untreated municipal or pharmaceutical wastewater. Supplementary details were not uploaded.

Experimental design / conditions: Solvent desorption comparison; repeated adsorption/desorption runs
Reported result: 90% ethanol desorption was 98.87%, while distilled water desorbed 6.32%. Authors report 98.9% recovery of adsorbed Dox; 148.06 mg crystals obtained after ethanol elution/evaporation. Removal efficiency declined 22.66% in distilled water and 42.24% in seawater after first reuse; after third reuse the declines were 35% and 61.34%
Value / units: 98.87% desorption; 6.32% desorption; 148.06 mg crystals; reported declines in removal efficiency
Model / metric: Observed desorption, recovered mass and change in removal efficiency
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 10, §3.9, Fig. 7; PDF p. 11, §3.10; Fig. S4 referenced but not supplied
Caveat / follow-up: A decline in removal efficiency is not the same as absolute removal remaining. The supplementary spectrum and detailed balance are unavailable in this upload.

Adsorbent / material: Rice-straw biochar and ethanol elution/recrystallization process
Experimental design / conditions: Model assumes 200 kg biomass per batch, producing 38.46 kg biochar; annual operation 7920 h and annual production 76,115.38 kg biochar
Reported result: Authors estimate biochar preparation cost $0.94/kg, annual influent-treatment/recovery operating cost $123,000 and total process cost $195,000. Under their model, a $41/kg recovered-Dox sale price would be enough for profitability versus a cited $94/kg price
Value / units: $0.94/kg biochar; $123,000/year operating cost; $195,000 process cost; $41–94/kg Dox price scenarios
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 11, §3.11, Fig. 8; Table S2 is referenced but not included
Caveat / follow-up: Model-dependent estimate, not a plant demonstration or harmonized comparison. Material balance assumes high Dox concentration (250 mg/L); SI cost breakdown unavailable.

Experimental design / conditions: CHNS, XRF, Raman, XRD, zeta potential, FTIR and BET/BJH discussed
Reported result: Authors report C 41.06%, N 9.01%, H 1.48%, S 0.32%; XRF reports SiO₂ 36.87%. BET/BJH text reports surface area 8.931 m²/g (adsorption branch) and 8.563 m²/g (desorption branch), pore-size values 3.408 and 5.613 nm. Non-ionic interactions and possible π–π/van der Waals interactions are proposed
Value / units: Composition percentages; m²/g; nm; qualitative mechanism
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 5, §3.2; PDF p. 6, Fig. 2; PDF pp. 5–6, §3.3, Fig. 3
Caveat / follow-up: The authors' mechanism is an interpretation, not definitive proof of covalent bonding. Supplementary Fig. S1 is missing. Table 4 reports thermodynamic units requiring verification before reuse.

Adsorbent / material: Pine bark, oak ash from combustion of oak chips, mussel shell by-product
Experimental design / conditions: Binary tests: one antibiotic held at 200 µmol/L, second varied 0–600 µmol/L; 1 g sorbent with 40 mL 0.005 M CaCl₂, shaken 24 h. Desorption in 40 mL 0.005 M CaCl₂ for another 24 h; measurements triplicated
Reported result: Six pairwise binary combinations tested across three sorbents; uptake calculated as initial minus equilibrium concentration. Tests are controlled CaCl₂ batch experiments
Value / units: 1 g / 40 mL; 0.005 M CaCl₂; 24 h adsorption + 24 h desorption
Caveat / follow-up: Study context is potential sorbent addition/retention in affected soils/agrosystems, not direct wastewater-plant treatment.

Adsorbent / material: Oak ash; pine bark; mussel shell
Experimental design / conditions: Table 1 characterization of the three bioadsorbents
Reported result: pHwater: oak ash 11.31, pine bark 3.99, mussel shell 9.39. Organic matter: oak ash 13.23%, pine bark 48.7%, mussel shell 11.43%
Caveat / follow-up: Different material chemistry and pH affect adsorption; these sorbents are not interchangeable material classes.

Adsorbent / material: Pine bark, oak ash, mussel shell
Experimental design / conditions: Simple systems at 200 µmol/L; binary tests with one antibiotic fixed at 200 µmol/L and a second up to 600 µmol/L
Reported result: In simple systems, oak ash adsorbed ~100% CTC, ~90% TC and ~80% OTC. Pine bark was strongest overall, with adsorption generally >90% in most binary cases. Mussel-shell adsorption was <25% for OTC and CTC in simple systems
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 4, §3.2, Fig. 1
Caveat / follow-up: Percentages reflect the study's high micromolar feeds and 24 h batch contact; do not rank against unlike matrices/conditions.

Target / co-contaminant: TC, OTC, CTC in binary systems
Adsorbent / material: Pine bark, oak ash, mussel shell
Experimental design / conditions: One antibiotic held at 200 µmol/L and the second increased to 600 µmol/L
Reported result: Between simple and highest-dose binary systems, adsorption differences on pine bark were generally <8%; oak-ash differences ranged from 11% to 65%, depending on the antibiotic pair
Caveat / follow-up: Differences apply to specified binary pairs; do not turn them into a universal competition coefficient.

Adsorbent / material: Pine bark, oak ash, mussel shell
Experimental design / conditions: Desorption measured following another 24 h shake in 40 mL 0.005 M CaCl₂; triplicate measurements
Reported result: Authors report desorption <5% in most cases for pine bark/oak ash and generally high desorption for mussel shell; one mussel-shell binary comparison reports up to 100% desorption of one antibiotic previously adsorbed
Value / units: <5% in most pine bark/oak ash cases; up to 100% in a specific mussel-shell comparison
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 6, §3.4, Fig. 2; PDF pp. 8–9, §3.5, Fig. 5
Caveat / follow-up: 100% is a specific competitive case, not a general statement. The ternary comparison reuses earlier published data.

Adsorbent / material: Pine bark, oak ash, mussel shell
Experimental design / conditions: Modified Freundlich model for binary systems; Murali–Aylmore model used for pairwise competition
Reported result: Modified Freundlich fits had R² >0.95 in most, but not all cases; authors report α₂₁ indexes could not be estimated because associated model fits were unsatisfactory. Authors propose pH/speciation and H-bonding/carboxyl-group interactions for pine bark and possible Ca²⁺ bridging for alkaline oak ash
Value / units: R² >0.95 in most cases; α₂₁ not estimated for unsatisfactory fits; qualitative mechanism interpretation
Model / metric: Modified Freundlich and Murali–Aylmore model fit; proposed mechanisms
Caveat / follow-up: Mechanisms are the authors' interpretations. Model parameters from unsatisfactory/non-adjustable fits should not be treated as comparable capacities.
